passage: For four months Irawati had done everything right: the same wake time, no phone after ten, a wind-down routine, no evening tea. Still she lay awake until three and woke exhausted, and the board exams were six weeks away. Her mother Aadhya had watched the dark circles and the swings between hope and despair. "It's not lack of effort," Aadhya said one Saturday. "Let's ask a doctor to look at this properly." Irawati hesitated. "Will they think I'm making it up?" "They'll listen." The doctor took a long history, asked about her days, and arranged a check-up and a follow-up visit. There was no quick answer, but for the first time Irawati felt that someone whose job this was had taken it seriously. She kept her routine while waiting.

passage:
For four months, Suraj had done everything right in their Kolkata flat. Phone out of the room at ten. Same wake time every day, curtains open, a morning walk to the park. His sister Kashish had even helped him draw a sleep chart.

But the chart told a strange story. He was in bed by 10:30 every night and still lay awake for hours. Mornings, he felt as if he hadn't slept at all. In class he nodded off twice in one week.

"You've done all the habits," Kashish said one evening, looking at the chart. "This isn't about trying harder anymore."

Their mother agreed. The next Saturday she took Suraj to the family doctor, with the chart in his hand. The doctor read it carefully, asked a lot of questions, and said, "Good that you came. Let's look into this properly."

Suraj walked out feeling lighter, even without answers yet.

qa.q: Where did Suraj walk every morning?
qa.a: To the park, as part of his morning routine.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel walking out of the doctor's clinic?
qa.a: He felt lighter and relieved, glad to be taken seriously even without answers yet.

qa.q: What would you tell Suraj if new habits ever stop working again?
qa.a: Keep noting what happens and talk to the doctor again, because sleep trouble that goes on despite good habits is for a professional to check.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt looking at the chart that evening?
qa.a: Kashish probably felt worried and caring, sensing that her brother's effort was real and that more help was needed.

grounding: Shows a family taking a student to the doctor after months of good habits still leave him sleepless, treating persistent sleep trouble as something for a professional.

"Lalremsiami, you're falling asleep on your book again," Urmila said, sitting beside her on the hostel bed.

"I don't understand it. I've done everything. Phone out at ten. Up at six. No tea after lunch. For three months."

"And?"

"And I still lie awake. Then I'm exhausted all day." Her voice cracked. "I thought if I tried hard enough..."

Urmila frowned. "Three months is a long time. This might not be something you fix by trying harder. Have you told your parents?"

"I didn't want to worry them."

"They'd want to know. And the warden could help you see the school doctor."

That evening, Lalremsiami called home. Her mother listened and said, "We'll take you to the doctor on Saturday. You did the right thing telling us." Then Urmila walked with her to the warden's office to ask about the school doctor too.

How did Lalremsiami feel when her voice cracked?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and discouraged, even a little ashamed, because hard work hadn't fixed the problem.

qa.q: What would you advise Lalremsiami to bring to the doctor?
qa.a: A simple note of her bedtimes, wake times and how she feels each day, so the doctor can see the pattern clearly.

qa.q: How might Urmila see her friend's struggle?
qa.a: Urmila likely feels worried and caring, which is why she urges telling the parents and walks with Lalremsiami to the warden.

grounding: Shows a student whose sleep trouble persists despite months of good habits, and a family arranging a doctor, treating persistent trouble as something professionals should assess.
